<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with clean structure, direct A1/A2 answers, and no fake sourcing. B won the decisive exchanges: the coercion-symmetry "proves too much" argument (if refusal is impossible because services are essential, an opt-in yes is coerced by the same logic) was never fully neutralized—A's decoupling answer ("you keep the email, the maps, the search") was asserted as a promise, and B correctly noted nothing in the motion guarantees it. B also blunted A's best evidence by reframing the Apple ATT refusal as a costless "no" that revealed nothing, and turned A's "shared consent infrastructure" concession into an entrenchment point ("login standards are Google and Apple buttons"). A landed strong counterpunches—the loyalty-program flip in closing and the "note what the question concedes" move in Rebuttal 2—but B had pre-answered them (users do say yes: personalization toggles, loyalty cards, free-tier choices). B's closing crystallization of PRO's contradictions gave the cleaner reason to vote, while A's closing relied on a flip B had already absorbed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5-B4.7: B's exposure that PRO's decoupling promise ("you keep the email, the maps, the search") has no mechanism in the motion, combined with the login-standards-as-giant-capture rejoinder, plus the closing summary "PRO needs consent to be impossible yet achievable, refusal ruinous yet costless, giants the disease yet the cure." This was the sharpest sustained pressure of the debate and A never fully recovered from it.</best_rebuttal>
